body: {"total":6,"records":[{"title":"Group medical visits for adults with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis","authors":"Adeyinka-Solberg M, Fairbairn-Otieno C, Leclerc-Mahmoud S","year":2020,"venue":"Primary Care Diabetes Reviews","doi":"10.5555/pcdr.2020.0072","providerType":"review","abstract":"We included 26 randomised trials (4,410 adults) comparing group medical visits, in which a clinician sees 6 to 15 patients together for education and individual review, with usual individual care for type 2 diabetes. At 6 to 12 months, group visits lowered HbA1c by a mean of 4.4 mmol/mol (95 percent CI 2.7 to 6.1), with no clear effect on blood pressure or weight. Heterogeneity was substantial, and effects were larger in trials with more sessions and higher baseline HbA1c. Only eight trials reported patient-reported outcomes, and attendance was reported inconsistently."},{"title":"Group consultations versus usual care for type 2 diabetes in general practice: a cluster-randomised trial in 24 practices","authors":"Mortensen-Achebe L, Dubois-Nakamura T, Okafor-Lindqvist J","year":2023,"venue":"Journal of Primary Care Trials","doi":"10.5555/jpct.2023.0198","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"Twenty-four practices were randomly allocated to offer group consultations or usual individual reviews to adults with type 2 diabetes and HbA1c of 58 mmol/mol or more. At 12 months the mean difference in HbA1c was 2.1 mmol/mol in favour of group consultations (95 percent CI -0.6 to 4.8), and diabetes distress scores improved more in the group arm. Only 61 percent of invited patients attended at least half the sessions. Nurse time per patient was 35 percent lower, but patients who worked full time attended least."},{"title":"Outcomes of patients attending diabetes group visits compared with non-attenders: a retrospective records study","authors":"Bhattacharya-Cole R, Weston-Adebayo P","year":2018,"venue":"Practice Diabetes Care","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using records from four practices, we compared 412 adults with type 2 diabetes who attended group visits with 1,630 who did not. Attenders had a 6 mmol/mol lower HbA1c after a year, but they were younger, more often retired and had better HbA1c before their first group visit. After adjustment for age and baseline HbA1c, the difference fell to 2 mmol/mol. The authors note that motivation, which the records do not capture, probably explains part of the remaining difference, and they recommend a randomised comparison."},{"title":"Company, comparison and privacy: patients' experiences of diabetes group visits","authors":"Nwosu-Hartmann G, Petrov-Achterberg V","year":2021,"venue":"Chronic Illness Experience","doi":"10.5555/cie.2021.0144","providerType":"qualitative research","abstract":"We interviewed 31 adults with type 2 diabetes who had been offered group visits in three practices. Many valued meeting others with the same condition and learning from their experiences. Some felt uncomfortable discussing weight or results in front of neighbours and preferred individual reviews. People who spoke limited English and people with shift work found it hardest to take part. Participants suggested short individual time within each session and evening options. Interviews were conducted by practice staff, which may have limited criticism, and nobody who had declined the offer outright was interviewed."},{"title":"Clinician time and costs of group visits for type 2 diabetes in primary care: a cost analysis","authors":"Grimaldi-Owusu F, Sandhu-Lindgren K","year":2019,"venue":"Health Economics in Primary Care","doi":"10.5555/hepc.2019.0051","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We costed group visits in six practices over one year using staff diaries and appointment records. Each 90-minute session for about ten patients used a nurse and a GP for part of the session. Clinician time per patient was 28 percent lower than for equivalent individual reviews, but administrative time for booking and reminders was higher. Savings depended on sessions being at least 70 percent full. The analysis did not include patient time or travel costs. Sessions that were less than half full cost more per patient than individual reviews."},{"title":"Contamination in individually randomised trials of group-based care in general practice: a methods study","authors":"Holloway-Tanaka D, Eze-Marchetti A","year":2016,"venue":"Trials Methods Review","doi":"10.5555/tmr.2016.0020","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examined 18 individually randomised trials of group-based interventions delivered in general practice. In nine, the same clinicians delivered both arms, and six reported changes in usual care during the trial that could dilute the comparison. Clustering within groups in the intervention arm was ignored in 11 trials, which overstated precision. We recommend partially nested analyses, separating clinicians where feasible, and reporting what usual care looked like during the trial. Only four trials described usual care during the trial period, and none measured whether patients in the comparison arm heard about the groups from other patients."}]}
